figures.caption: Figure 1. Schematic illustration of QSSSR-based Li−S cells with organosulfur mediation effects. (a) Li−S cell in conventional diglyme (G2) electrolytes exhibits dissolution−precipitation sulfur reactions that induces pronounced polysulfides dissolution/shuttle and lithium anode corrosion. (b) Li−S cell in proposed siloxane-based electrolyte (with DIP as reaction mediator) enables global QSSSRs with fast kinetics, eliminating LiPSs dissolution/shuttle and promoting dendrite-free deposition for stable lithium anode. reactions of sulfur and lithium electrodes are both governed by the electrolyte’s solvation structure. figures.caption: Figure 2. Electrolyte structure characterizations. (a) Raman spectra of LiTFSI-G2 and LiTFSI-FPDS/G2 electrolytes with TFSI−bands. (b) 7Li spectra showing Li+ coordination environments and fwhm values for LiTFSI-G2 and LiTFSI-FPDS/G2 electrolytes. (c−d) Results of AIMD simulations for (c) LiTFSI-FPDS/G2 and (d) LiTFSI-G2, coordination numbers (right) and Li−O radial distribution functions (RDF, left). (e) Coordination numbers of Li−O in the first solvation shell for LiTFSI-G2 and LiTFSI-FPDS/G2 electrolytes. (f) AIMD simulation snapshots of Li+ solvation clusters for LiTFSI-FPDS/G2. Lithium atoms (green) are highlighted to delineate the coordination environment, while other atoms (sulfur, fluorine, oxygen, nitrogen, carbon, and silicon) are rendered with smaller diameters for enhanced clarity.
